# Energy Management and Audit (MOPEC) — Mid-Sem Analysis (30 Marks)

**Subject Code:** BE05000431  
**Exam:** Progressive Assessment, September 2026  
**Scope:** All 5 units (confirmed from syllabus document title)  
**College:** GEC Bharuch — Electrical Engineering  

> [!WARNING]
> **No PYQ papers exist** for this subject — it's a new syllabus. All priority assignments below are based on marks weightage, GTU exam format patterns, and topic structure analysis. Confidence is lower than a PYQ-backed analysis. Adjust if your professor gives any hints about question patterns.

---

## 1. Syllabus Breakdown — What You're Actually Responsible For

### Unit 1 — Energy Scenario, Policy & Legislative Framework (18% weight)

**Type:** Pure theory — definitions, acts, schemes, policies. Zero numericals.

| # | Topic | Question Type | Study Priority |
|---|-------|--------------|----------------|
| 1 | Energy scenario in India & Gujarat: sector-wise consumption patterns | Short answer / MCQ | 🔴 High |
| 2 | EC Act 2001 — key provisions, designated consumers, penalties | Long answer (list/explain) | 🔴 High |
| 3 | EC Amendment Act 2022 — Carbon Credit Trading, Non-Fossil Obligations (RCO/RPO), sustainability building codes | Short/Long answer | 🟡 Medium |
| 4 | BEE: structure, PAT scheme, ESCerts, Standards & Labelling, UJALA | Long answer (explain with examples) | 🔴 High |
| 5 | NMEEE (National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency) | Short answer | 🟡 Medium |
| 6 | State-level: GUVNL, GEDA, Gujarat Solar/Wind policies, GERC tariff orders | Short answer / MCQ | 🟡 Medium |
| 7 | Electricity Act 2003 — relevance to metering & distribution | Short answer | 🟢 Low |
| 8 | India's COP-26 commitments and SDG 7 | Short answer / MCQ | 🟢 Low |

**What makes this unit dangerous:** It's dense with acronyms and act names. GTU loves asking "Explain EC Act 2001 with key provisions" or "Explain PAT scheme" as 4-7 mark questions. If you can't recall the specific provisions/penalties/year details, you lose marks fast.

---

### Unit 2 — Electrical Energy Audit: Methodology, Instruments & Procedures (20% weight)

**Type:** Mix — mostly theory with some calculation-based topics (power factor, load factor, demand factor, SEC).

| # | Topic | Question Type | Study Priority |
|---|-------|--------------|----------------|
| 1 | Definition & need of energy audit | Short answer (2-3 marks) | 🔴 High |
| 2 | Types of audit: preliminary (walk-through), detailed (diagnostic), investment-grade | Long answer (compare/contrast) | 🔴 High |
| 3 | Energy audit team, scope & boundaries | Short answer | 🟡 Medium |
| 4 | Data collection, historical bill analysis, load profiling | Short/Long answer | 🟡 Medium |
| 5 | Electricity tariff structures: ToD, ToU, HT/LT tariffs | Short answer + possible numerical | 🔴 High |
| 6 | EnPIs, benchmarking, Specific Energy Consumption (SEC) | Numerical + theory | 🔴 High |
| 7 | BEE-certified EM & EA: qualifications, eligibility, accreditation, statutory duties under EC Act | Long answer | 🟡 Medium |
| 8 | Instruments: energy analyzers (IEC 61557-12, IS 15884), clamp meters, data loggers, IR cameras, lux meters, power quality analyzers | List/explain with application | 🔴 High |
| 9 | Measurement: kWh, kVAh, kVArh, power factor, load factor, demand factor | **Numerical** (definite) | 🔴 High |

**This unit has the highest weight (20%) and the most exam-friendly content.** Definitions, comparisons (types of audit), instrument lists, and simple calculations (power factor, load factor, demand factor) — all easy to frame as questions.

---

### Unit 3 — Power Quality Assessment and Improvement (18% weight)

**Type:** Theory + Numericals. Harmonics and power factor improvement are classic numerical territory.

| # | Topic | Question Type | Study Priority |
|---|-------|--------------|----------------|
| 1 | Power quality — definition, importance, financial cost of poor PQ | Short answer | 🔴 High |
| 2 | Voltage sags/swells: causes, classification (IEEE 1159) | Short answer | 🟡 Medium |
| 3 | Harmonics: generation by non-linear loads (VFDs, UPS, rectifiers) | Theory (explain mechanism) | 🔴 High |
| 4 | THD, harmonic spectrum; limits per IEEE 519-2022, IEC 61000-3-2, IEC 61000-3-12 | Theory + possible numerical | 🔴 High |
| 5 | Harmonic filters — passive, active, hybrid | Compare/contrast (long answer) | 🟡 Medium |
| 6 | Voltage unbalance: causes & effects on motors (IEC 60034-26) | Short answer | 🟡 Medium |
| 7 | Flicker: PST, PLT; IEC 61000-4-15 | Short answer | 🟢 Low |
| 8 | Power factor improvement: effect on losses & tariff penalty | **Numerical** + theory | 🔴 High |
| 9 | Capacitor bank sizing & placement (IS 13925 / IEEE 18) | **Numerical** | 🔴 High |

**Key numerical areas:** Capacitor bank sizing for PF improvement, THD calculation, and loss reduction from PF correction. These are the most likely numerical questions from this unit.

---

### Unit 4 — Energy Efficiency of Electrical Equipment & Systems (20% weight)

**Type:** Heavy mix — theory + numericals. Affinity laws and motor efficiency are classic GTU numerical topics.

| # | Topic | Question Type | Study Priority |
|---|-------|--------------|----------------|
| 1 | Motors: efficiency classes IE1–IE4 (IS 12615 / IEC 60034-30-1) | Short answer / table | 🔴 High |
| 2 | Motor right-sizing, efficiency testing (IEEE 112), rewinding losses | Theory + possible numerical | 🟡 Medium |
| 3 | VFDs: energy savings, selection criteria, harmonic impact | Long answer | 🔴 High |
| 4 | Pumps & fans: affinity laws, system curve, BEP | **Numerical** (almost certain) | 🔴 High |
| 5 | Specific energy consumption of pumps/fans; audit methodology (IS 9137) | Theory + numerical | 🟡 Medium |
| 6 | Feeder-level loss calculation, capacitor placement optimization, reconductoring economics | **Numerical** | 🟡 Medium |
| 7 | Rooftop solar PV: energy yield estimation (CUF, performance ratio) | **Numerical** | 🔴 High |
| 8 | Net metering (Gujarat policy, IS 16221) | Theory | 🟡 Medium |
| 9 | BESS for peak-shaving (IEC 62933) | Theory | 🟢 Low |

**Affinity laws are a near-certain numerical.** The relationship P₂/P₁ = (N₂/N₁)³ is one of the most commonly tested formulas in energy management. Solar PV yield estimation (using CUF and performance ratio) is another strong numerical candidate.

---

### Unit 5 — DSM, Supply-Side Efficiency & Grid Technologies (16% weight)

**Type:** Mostly conceptual/theory. Lowest weight.

| # | Topic | Question Type | Study Priority |
|---|-------|--------------|----------------|
| 1 | DSM: objectives & strategies — load levelling, valley-filling, load shifting, peak-load management | Long answer (list & explain) | 🔴 High |
| 2 | ToD tariff & smart metering (IS 16444); prepaid metering | Short answer | 🟡 Medium |
| 3 | Smart grid: AMI, demand response, Volt/VAR optimization | Short/Long answer | 🟡 Medium |
| 4 | Power distribution feeder audit | Short answer | 🟢 Low |

**Smallest unit by content and weight.** DSM strategies (load levelling, valley-filling, load shifting, peak-load management) is the one high-priority topic — it's a clean 4-7 mark question: "Explain DSM strategies with load curve diagrams."

## 3. 🎯 Strategy A: Score 20/30 (~8-10 hours)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This is a survival strategy. It targets the highest-weight, easiest-to-score topics across all 5 units.

### Study Order (follow this sequence):

| 1 | EC Act 2001 — key provisions, designated consumers, penalties | 1 | 45 min | 3-4 marks |

**What it is:** Good power quality means delivering a perfect, smooth sine wave at exactly 50Hz and exactly 230V (or 415V for 3-phase). 

**The Financial Cost of Poor PQ (Exam Question):**
If the sine wave gets distorted, companies lose money in three ways:
1. **Hardware damage:** Motors overheat and burn out due to negative sequence currents.
2. **Production downtime:** Sensitive PLCs and computers reboot randomly when voltage drops.
3. **Tariff penalties:** Utilities (like GUVNL) charge massive penalties if poor power quality (like bad power factor) pollutes the main grid.

### 2. Harmonics (The Core Concept)
A harmonic is an unwanted, extra electrical frequency riding on top of your standard 50Hz power. 
* 1st Harmonic (Fundamental) = 50Hz (This is the good power you want).
* 3rd Harmonic = 150Hz (3 × 50)
* 5th Harmonic = 250Hz (5 × 50)

When these extra frequencies mix with your 50Hz wave, they distort the perfect sine wave into a jagged, messy shape. 

**What causes them? (Write exactly these three in the exam):**
They are caused by **Non-Linear Loads**. A linear load (like an old incandescent bulb or a simple heater) draws current smoothly. A non-linear load chops the current into pieces to convert AC to DC or change speeds. 
Your syllabus highlights three specific culprits:
1. **VFDs (Variable Frequency Drives):** They chop the wave to control motor speed.
2. **Rectifiers:** They chop the wave to convert AC to DC.
3. **UPS Systems:** The internal switching creates massive distortion.

### 3. THD (Total Harmonic Distortion)
This is how we measure the damage. THD is the ratio of all the "bad" harmonic currents compared to the "good" fundamental current.

**The Formula:**
`THD = [ √(I₃² + I₅² + I₇² ...) / I₁ ] × 100%`
*(Where I₁ is the 50Hz current, and I₃, I₅ are the unwanted harmonic currents).*

**The Limits:** You don't need to memorize the exact tables, but you must write that **IEEE 519-2022** and **IEC 61000-3-2** are the international standards that set the maximum allowable THD (usually keeping voltage THD under 5%).

### 4. Harmonic Filters (The Fix)
If a factory has high THD, the Energy Auditor will recommend filters. The syllabus requires you to know three types:

1. **Passive Filters:** Built using simple Inductors (L) and Capacitors (C). 
   * *How they work:* Tuned to trap one specific frequency (e.g., trapping only the 5th harmonic). 
   * *Pros/Cons:* Cheap and reliable, but they are fixed. If the factory adds new machines, the filter won't adapt.
2. **Active Filters:** Built using power electronics (IGBTs).
   * *How they work:* It constantly measures the bad harmonics and instantly injects an "anti-harmonic" wave (exact opposite shape) to cancel them out, just like noise-canceling headphones.
   * *Pros/Cons:* Very expensive, but highly adaptable to changing factory loads.
3. **Hybrid Filters:** A combination of both. Uses cheap passive filters to handle the bulk of the heavy harmonics, and a small active filter to clean up the rest. (Most cost-effective for large plants).

### 5. Sags, Swells, and Unbalance (Definitions)
* **Voltage Sag (Dip):** The voltage drops by 10% to 90% for a few milliseconds. *Cause:* Starting a massive industrial motor (it pulls 6x normal current, draining voltage from everything else).
* **Voltage Swell:** The voltage spikes up for a few milliseconds. *Cause:* Suddenly turning off a massive load, leaving excess voltage in the system.
* **Voltage Unbalance:** In a 3-phase system, the voltages in the R, Y, and B phases are not exactly equal (e.g., 415V, 400V, 410V). *Effect:* (IEC 60034-26 standard) This causes severe overheating in 3-phase induction motors because it creates opposing magnetic fields inside the stator.

***

**The Counter-Argument (Where textbook theory fails in real audits):**
In exams, installing an Active Harmonic Filter is the perfect answer to THD. In real life, Active Filters consume a significant amount of power just to run their own electronics (switching losses). An auditor must calculate if the energy saved by cleaning the harmonics is actually greater than the energy the active filter consumes. If it isn't, a simple Passive Filter is the better financial choice.
